(1) the interaction of subducted lithosphere with the mantle wedge can produce a variety of flow patterns that are sensitive to the nature of the residuum and (2) the resulting patterns of melt production and transport in the mantle wedge can reproduce many of the observed characteristics of volcanism in the Cascade-Yellowstone region.

(1) The presence of residuum in a subduction zone can influence the style of mantle circulation, and (2) The interaction of residuum with the subducting slab and overlying mantle wedge can influence the style and magnitude of melt generation and eruption.

(1) the interaction of a subduction zone with residuum left over from a major flood basalt event can produce bimodal melt production and a wedge with chemical heterogeneity that can influence the location of volcanoes; and (2) the age-progressive melting pattern of the SRP region may be difficult to explain with a non-plume model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of melt-induced chemical heterogeneities in the mantle and the role of these heterogeneities on the formation of volcanic tracks.
the role of melt-induced heterogeneity and residuum in subducting slabs on the dynamics of subduction zones, and how these heterogeneities may be expressed at the surface as volcanic tracks.
the influence of melt production and extraction on the subsequent circulation patterns in the mantle wedge.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our experiments do not rule out a plume explanation for the SRP and Yellowstone region but that they do indicate that a plume explanation may not be necessary.
a plume model is not required for the HLP-SRP region, but that a plume is not ruled out either.
the lab experiments do not support a plume explanation for the Cascades-Yellowstone volcanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Cascadia subducting slab and the CSFB residuum are the dominant factors in controlling the style of mantle circulation and the resulting volcanism.
the CSFB residuum is a viable explanation for the age-progressive tracks in the HLP, but it does not adequately account for the age progression of the SRP tracks.
the mantle-residuum interactions in our models can explain many aspects of the Cascades system, and that the SRP remains an enigma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mantle residuum from a major melt event can be a major player in subduction-driven convection.
mantle heterogeneity can drive complex, non-uniform melt generation and transport patterns.
the CSFB event is the most likely source of the residuum that is driving the circulation and melting beneath the HLA and the SRP.
